title: Inherent Turbulence Immunity of Vector Vortex Beams in Free Space Quantum Key Distribution
abstract: Orbital angular momentum (OAM) multiplexing provides an infinite-dimensional discrete Hilbert space ideally suited for high-capacity free-space quantum key distribution (QKD). Nevertheless, pure scalar spatial modes carrying topological charge ($|\ell| \ge 1$) undergo severe decoherence when transmitted through terrestrial atmospheric turbulence. Turbulent refractive-index eddies split high-order vortex singularities, induce catastrophic intermodal crosstalk across adjacent topological channels, and rapidly drive the quantum bit error rate (QBER) well above the unconditional 11% security threshold associated with individual cloning attacks. Here, we demonstrate that hybrid polarization-OAM entangled states, known as vector vortex beams (VVBs), provide intrinsic, hardware-free immunity against turbulent perturbations. Because the optical anisotropy of terrestrial air is exceedingly small ($Δn < 10^{-9}$), refractive-index fluctuations couple symmetrically to orthogonal circular polarization modes as an identical common-mode scalar phase screen that cancels in the relative polarization-phase degree of freedom. By numerically propagating modal fields through modified power-spectral phase screens over turbulence strengths ranging from $D/r_0 = 0$ to $3.0$, we show that the VVB encoding protocol suppresses the asymptotic QBER from 42.0% to 4.8%, yielding an error-suppression factor of approximately 11.6 without requiring active adaptive optics or deformable mirrors.
summary: This paper demonstrates that using Vector Vortex Beams (VVBs) for quantum key distribution provides inherent immunity to atmospheric turbulence, a major hurdle for free-space quantum links. By exploiting the symmetry of terrestrial air's refractive index fluctuations, the VVB encoding suppresses the error rate significantly without needing complex, active adaptive optics. This breakthrough suggests a pathway for robust, practical quantum communication over atmospheric channels.
main_problem: High-capacity free-space Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) using Orbital Angular Momentum (OAM) multiplexing is severely degraded by atmospheric turbulence, causing decoherence and exceeding security thresholds.
main_result: Vector Vortex Beams (VVBs) provide intrinsic, hardware-free immunity against turbulent perturbations, suppressing the Quantum Bit Error Rate (QBER) from 42.0% down to 4.8%.
method: The authors used numerical propagation simulations to model the evolution of VVB states through phase screens representing atmospheric turbulence.
model_or_system: The system involves quantum optical links transmitting structured light (VVBs) through a turbulent atmosphere. The VVB state is a hybrid polarization-OAM entangled state, and the turbulence is modeled by refractive-index fluctuations.
key_observables: Quantum Bit Error Rate (QBER), VVB state survival probability, and Quantum State Fidelity (F).
important_parameters: Turbulence strength parameter $D/r_0$ (ranging from 0 to 3.0); the security threshold of 11% for QBER.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the optical anisotropy of terrestrial air is very small ($\Delta n < 10^{-9}$), which allows the turbulent phase screen to act as an identical common-mode scalar phase screen that cancels in the relative polarization-phase degree of freedom.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the spatial scrambling of pure scalar OAM beams versus the preserved polarization structure of VVBs after turbulence, and plot the QBER and Fidelity decay as a function of turbulence strength.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the problem of turbulence degrading OAM-based QKD. It then introduces VVBs as a solution, detailing the physical mechanism (common-mode phase cancellation) and presenting numerical simulations comparing the performance of scalar beams versus VVBs across varying turbulence strengths.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the practical limitations of quantum communication in real-world environments by proposing a structural encoding (VVB) that leverages fundamental symmetries to achieve passive robustness against environmental noise, which is highly relevant to quantum networking.
